sermon:
## The Gospel That Bears Fruit: The Living Word in Colossians 1:1-14
*Why Paul thanks God for a church he had never met*

**Text:** Colossians 1:1-14 · **Supporting:** Mark 4:8; Isaiah 55:11; Philippians 1:6; Ephesians 1:17-18; Colossians 2:6-7

Paul wrote this letter to a church he had never visited, in a town he had never walked, to people he knew only by report. And the first thing he does is give thanks. Not for their numbers. Not for their giftedness. He gives thanks because something living had taken root in them, and living things do one thing: they grow. We have inherited a version of faith that measures itself by intensity — how it feels on Sunday, how loud the room gets, how full the heart runs before it empties again by Tuesday. Paul measures something else. He measures fruit. And a man in a Roman prison, watching an empire that could crush a small church in an afternoon, stakes his whole confidence on the strange idea that the word about a crucified Jew was quietly outgrowing the empire.

### I. The Gospel Is a Living Thing That Grows (Colossians 1:1-8)

Paul opens not with instruction but with gratitude, and the object of his gratitude is startling. He thanks God for the Colossians' faith and love, which spring, he says, from something already deposited in them. "Of this you have heard before in the word of the truth, the gospel, which has come to you, as indeed in the whole world it is bearing fruit and increasing — as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth" (Colossians 1:5-6). Read that slowly. The gospel is not described as a message that was delivered and filed. It is described as an organism. It bears fruit. It increases. The Greek is agricultural — karpophoroumenon kai auxanomenon, fruit-bearing and growing — the same two words that stand behind the Lord's parable of the seed that fell on good soil and "produced grain, growing up and increasing" (Mark 4:8).

This matters because it relocates the source of Christian life outside of us. Paul is not congratulating the Colossians on their spiritual industry. He is telling them what the seed did once it landed. The word Isaiah heard from the mouth of God said the same thing: "So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose" (Isaiah 55:11). The gospel has a life of its own. It carries its own increase inside it, the way a seed carries the tree.

And there is a phrase here that is easy to read past. The gospel came to them "since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth" (Colossians 1:6). Heard and understood. Not heard and admired. Not heard and filed away as one option among the era's many spiritualities. The fruit begins on the day grace is understood, on the day a person grasps that God's favor is a gift and not a wage. That is the germination point — the moment the seed cracks open. A great deal of what passes for Christianity has heard the gospel a thousand times and never once understood the grace of God in truth, and so it has never borne anything, because a seed that is admired but never planted does exactly nothing. Understanding grace is the water on the seed.

And notice that Paul roots the whole thing in Epaphras, "our beloved fellow servant... a faithful minister of Christ" (Colossians 1:7), the man who first carried the word to Colossae. The gospel does not spread as an abstraction; it spreads through a named person who tells another named person. The living word travels on human feet. This is not incidental to the doctrine — it is the mechanism of the doctrine. The seed is scattered by hand.

- **A. The gospel came from outside them and took root inside them.** Epaphras carried it to Colossae. They did not generate it; they received it. The whole point of Paul's thanksgiving is that the fruit is evidence of a grace that arrived, not an achievement they produced.
- **B. What is alive grows, and what is dead only decorates.** The church has always been tempted to preserve the gospel like a relic under glass. Paul will have none of it. A gospel that is not spreading and deepening is a gospel someone has quietly buried.

### II. Paul Prays for Depth, Not Ease (Colossians 1:9-14)

Then Paul tells them how he prays, and it exposes how shallow most of our praying has become. "We have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding" (Colossians 1:9). Notice what he does not ask for. He does not ask that their circumstances improve. He does not ask that the pressure lift. He asks that they know God's will and, knowing it, "walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God" (Colossians 1:10). There are the two words again. Bearing fruit. Increasing. The prayer and the gospel share the same DNA.

This is the mind of a man who has learned that growth is the answer to suffering, not its opposite. Paul asks that they be "strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy" (Colossians 1:11). We would have asked God to remove the thing requiring endurance. Paul asks God to strengthen them for it. This is the same confidence he names to the Philippians: "he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6). The prayer that God's people would be rooted rather than rescued is a prayer only someone in chains can pray without flinching.

And there is a peculiar phrase Paul attaches to this endurance — "with joy, giving thanks to the Father" (Colossians 1:11-12). Endurance and joy in the same sentence. We treat those as opposites, as if joy were what we feel when the hard thing lifts. Paul binds them. The joy is not the absence of the weight; it is thankfulness underneath the weight, because the weight is not the whole story. A man learns to give thanks in the dark only when he knows the dark is not where he lives. Which is exactly why Paul turns, in the next breath, to what is already secured.

And then Paul lands where all his praying lands — in what God has already done. "He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins" (Colossians 1:13-14). Delivered. Transferred. Redeemed. Past tense, all of it. The prayer for growth stands on the ground of a rescue already accomplished. We do not grow in order to be transferred; we grow because we already were.

Read those verbs once more, because the whole shape of the Christian life is in their tense. Delivered. Transferred. The word for transferred, methistēmi, was the word an ancient king used for relocating a conquered population from one land to another — an entire people uprooted and resettled under a new sovereign. Paul says God did that to you. You did not emigrate from the domain of darkness by your own decision and effort, applying for citizenship in the kingdom of the Son. You were carried across the border by the King who conquered the territory you were held in. The fruit Paul thanks God for at the top of the chapter is simply what a resettled people begin to grow once they are planted in a new country under a new Lord. Growth is not the price of the rescue. It is the evidence that the rescue took.

- **A. He echoes what Paul asks for the Ephesians — that they be given "a spirit of wisdom... having the eyes of your hearts enlightened" (Ephesians 1:17-18).** The deepest Christian need is not more feeling but more sight. To see what is already true.
- **B. The fruit and the rescue are not rivals.** Paul holds them together. The fruit is the evidence of the rescue, never its price.

### III. Fruit We Cannot Fake in a Culture That Measures Everything

We live downstream of a church that learned to count what it could photograph. Attendance. Baptisms tallied in a bulletin. The metrics of a movement measured like a quarterly report. And here is my own confession: I have stood in front of a congregation and felt the pull to report growth I could name in numbers, because numbers are easier to preach than fruit is to grow. I have wanted the crowd more than I have wanted the crop. Fruit is slow. Fruit is quiet. Fruit ripens in a life over years and cannot be manufactured for a report.

Consider what happened when the numbers failed. In 1799, in the aftermath of a bloodied French Revolution, a European church looked exhausted and outnumbered, and a generation concluded that Christianity was finishing. It was in exactly that decade that a former slave-ship captain turned Anglican pastor named John Newton was quietly discipling a young member of Parliament, and that William Carey had just sailed for India believing the gospel was a seed that would outgrow any empire that laughed at it. The counting said decline. The fruit said otherwise. The word was doing what Paul said it does — bearing fruit and increasing in the whole world — while the men who measured only the visible had already written the obituary.

We should be honest about why the measuring is so seductive, because it is not simple vanity. A number can be reported to a board, defended in a meeting, compared against last year, and celebrated on a screen. Fruit can do none of that. Fruit is the slow ripening of a marriage that did not end, the man who forgave the father who left, the woman who stopped organizing her life around a wound and did not tell anyone why. It does not photograph. It cannot be aggregated into a slide. And a church anxious for evidence that it matters will always drift toward the thing it can display, because the visible reassures and the fruit only waits. The tragedy is not that we count. The tragedy is what counting trains us to stop looking for.

So the question this text puts to a results-driven church is not "How large are you?" It is "What is growing that you did not plant?" Because the gospel that came to Colossae is the same gospel that came to you, and it does not need your management. It needs your soil. Christ said the seed grows "he knows not how" (Mark 4:27), and that ignorance is not a failure of faith. It is the mercy of a gospel that does not depend on us to keep it alive. Paul thanks God, not the Colossians, because he knows exactly whose life is at work in them. "As you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him" (Colossians 2:6-7).

- **A. A culture that measures everything will measure the wrong things in the church too.** We inherited its instruments and forgot they cannot weigh what matters. Fruit is not a number.
- **B. The gospel bears fruit through Christ, in you, whether or not anyone is counting.** The rescue is His; the growth is His; the harvest is His. Ours is to abide in the soil where the seed already fell.

The gospel grows where it lands.

## The Image of the Invisible God: The Supremacy of Christ in Colossians 1:15-23
*The hymn that answers the question underneath every other question*

**Text:** Colossians 1:15-23 · **Supporting:** John 1:3; Hebrews 1:3; Genesis 1:26-27; Romans 5:10; 2 Corinthians 4:4

There is a question underneath every other question a person ever asks. Not "Is there a God?" — that one is easier than we pretend. The harder question is "What is God like, if there is one?" A distant clockmaker. An impersonal force. A projection of our own need. The Colossians had been offered a crowded heaven of powers and principalities and cosmic intermediaries, a spiritual bureaucracy where Christ was one rung on a long ladder. Paul answers not with an argument but with a hymn, and the hymn does something the argument never could. It shows you the face. "He is the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). The invisible has an image, and the image has a name, and the name bled on a Roman cross outside a city wall.

### I. Christ Is the Firstborn Over All Creation (Colossians 1:15-17)

The word Paul reaches for is eikon — image. "He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible... all things were created through him and for him. And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:15-17). The word firstborn — prototokos — does not mean first-made, as the old heresies wanted it to. Paul immediately blocks that reading: everything was created through him, so he cannot be one of the created things. Firstborn is a word of rank, not of manufacture. It is the heir's word, the word for the son who holds the Father's authority over the whole estate.

And the estate is everything. "By him all things were created" — John says the same at the door of his Gospel: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made" (John 1:3). Paul stacks the categories deliberately: thrones, dominions, rulers, authorities. He is naming the very cosmic powers the Colossians had been taught to fear and appease, and he is filing every one of them under a Christ who made them. The powers you were told to negotiate with, he says, are subordinates He created and now outranks.

And Paul closes the phrase with a preposition that changes the meaning of existence itself. "All things were created through him and for him" (Colossians 1:16). Through him — He is the agent of creation. For him — He is its aim. The universe was not made and then handed a purpose later; it was made toward Christ, pointed at Him from the first word of Genesis. This is the answer to the question the modern mind cannot stop asking and cannot answer: what is it all for? Paul says the cosmos has a direction, and the direction has a face. A world made through Christ and for Christ is not a machine that happens to contain persons who invent their own meaning to survive the silence. It is a creation that was always leaning toward the one who would walk into it.

Then comes the line that holds the universe together — literally. "In him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:17). The Greek is sunestēken, the word for cohesion, for what keeps a thing from flying apart. Hebrews says he "upholds the universe by the word of his power" (Hebrews 1:3). This is not the deist's God who wound the clock and withdrew. This is a Christ whose sustaining attention is the reason the atom coheres this second. Withdraw it and there is no slow decline. There is nothing.

There is a further weight in the word firstborn that the ancient reader would have caught immediately. In the Old Testament, the firstborn is the one who receives the inheritance and represents the whole family before the father. When God calls Israel "my firstborn son" (Exodus 4:22), He is not saying Israel was the first nation manufactured; He is saying Israel holds a place of rank and inheritance. So when Paul calls Christ the firstborn over all creation, he is announcing an heir who owns the estate, not a product that rolled off the line first. The Colossian teachers wanted a Christ they could rank on a ladder of spiritual beings. Paul gives them a Christ who owns the ladder, the house it leans against, and the ground both stand on.

- **A. Christ is not inside creation as its finest part; He is over it as its maker and heir.** Genesis said humanity was made in God's image (Genesis 1:26-27). Paul says Christ is that image without qualification. He is what we were made to reflect.
- **B. Every power the world tells you to fear was made by the one who was crucified.** The cosmic bureaucracy is real, but it is staff, not sovereign.

### II. Through His Blood He Reconciles All Things (Colossians 1:18-23)

The hymn pivots without a seam from creation to the cross, and that seam is the whole gospel. The same Christ who made all things is "the head of the body, the church... that in everything he might be preeminent" (Colossians 1:18). And how does the maker of the cosmos assert His preeminence? Not with a display of the power that flung galaxies. "In him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross" (Colossians 1:19-20).

Stop on that. The one in whom all things hold together held together on a cross so that all things could be reconciled. The power that sustains the universe chose to be exhausted. Paul refuses to let cosmic glory float free of Golgotha. The blood is in the hymn. And the reconciliation is aimed, with precision, at people who were not neutral. "You, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds, he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death" (Colossians 1:21-22). Alienated. Hostile. That is not a description of a seeker with questions. That is a description of an enemy. Paul told the Romans the same: "while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10). We did not drift from God and get gently retrieved. We stood against Him, in the mind, in the deed, and He made peace by absorbing the war in His own body.

And Paul is careful about where the hostility lived — "alienated and hostile in mind" (Colossians 1:21). Not merely in behavior. In the mind, in the thinking, in the interior posture that curates reasons to keep God at a distance. This is the honest anatomy of unbelief, and it is more flattering to us than we deserve to admit: our estrangement from God is rarely a cold intellectual verdict and usually a warm defended preference. The mind that does not want God will always find the argument it needs. Reconciliation, then, is not God winning a debate. It is God reaching an enemy whose defenses were never really made of evidence.

Why could He alone do it? Because "the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God" (2 Corinthians 4:4). The image we suppressed is the image He restored — in Himself, and then in us.

- **A. Reconciliation is not God lowering the standard; it is God bearing the cost.** Peace was made by blood, not by a decision to overlook. The cross is where the maker paid.
- **B. The reconciled are held there "if indeed you continue in the faith, stable and steadfast" (Colossians 1:23).** The hymn ends in a summons to endure. Cosmic glory grounds ordinary perseverance.

And sit with the aim of the reconciliation, because Paul states it with a precision we tend to soften. The purpose was "to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him" (Colossians 1:22). Not merely forgiven. Not merely tolerated at the edge of the room. Presented — brought forward and displayed — as holy and without a single charge standing against you. The enemy who was hostile in mind is set before God faultless, and the fault was not overlooked but carried in the body of Christ on the cross. This is the whole distance the gospel travels: from alienated and hostile to holy and blameless, and it is crossed not by our slow moral repair but by the blood of a Christ in whom all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell. The maker of the powers made peace with His enemies. That is the hymn.

### III. The One Face in a Culture of a Thousand Powers

We were told the modern West outgrew the crowded heaven of the ancients. It did not. It renamed the powers. The market. The algorithm. The nation. The self. We no longer light incense to Fortune, but we still arrange our lives around forces we believe run the show and must be appeased — and I have preached from behind a pulpit while quietly appeasing the very powers I named from it, wanting the room's approval more than Christ's face. The Colossian error is not ancient. It is Tuesday. We keep Christ, and we add the powers, exactly as they did.

In 325, at the Council of Nicaea, the church faced a version of the Colossian question and refused to blink. Arius had taught that the Son was the highest of creatures — glorious, but made, the first thing God produced. It was a tidy solution, and it made Christ manageable, one rung near the top of the ladder rather than the ladder's Lord. The bishops who gathered under Constantine's summons wrote a single word against it that Paul's hymn had already required: homoousios, of one substance with the Father. They understood what Paul understood. If Christ is the firstborn over creation and not within it, then He is not one power among the powers you juggle. He is the one in whom they were all made and by whom they will all be judged.

So the practical weight of this hymn falls on a divided heart. You cannot hold together a life you have parceled out among a dozen small lords. That is why it comes apart. Paul's word for cohesion is the diagnosis of our disintegration: the things do not hold together because we have not let the one who holds all things hold us. The self you are exhausting yourself to sustain was never meant to be its own center of gravity. There is one image of the invisible God, and He made peace with His enemies by His blood, and He is asking to be the center your life coheres around instead of the ten you keep negotiating with. If your life is flying apart, it may be because you have asked everything to hold it together except the only one who can.

- **A. The powers are real, but they are created, and a created thing cannot be your center.** We keep adding lords and wondering why we cannot rest.
- **B. Christ reconciled enemies at the cost of His body; that is the only ground on which a hostile mind ever finds peace.** Not by improving. By being reconciled.

In Him all things hold together.

## Christ in You, the Hope of Glory: The Mystery Revealed in Colossians 1:24-2:5
*Why a man in chains called his suffering a joy*

**Text:** Colossians 1:24-2:5 · **Supporting:** Ephesians 3:8-9; Romans 16:25-26; Galatians 4:19; 1 Corinthians 1:24; Philippians 2:17

The ancient world was full of mysteries — secret knowledge, guarded rites, wisdom reserved for the initiated who had paid to be let in. The whole appeal of the mystery religions was exclusion: there was a hidden thing, and you did not have it, and you could, for a price and a vow of silence. Paul takes that word — mystērion — and detonates it. The mystery, he says, has been made known. It is not for sale and not kept secret. And when he tells you what it is, the whole architecture of the exclusive and the elite collapses, because the mystery hidden for ages turns out to be four words a child can hold: "Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:27). The secret the initiates could not buy is now the possession of a persecuted church in a nowhere town.

### I. Paul Suffers to Make the Mystery Known (Colossians 1:24-29)

Paul writes from prison, and he opens this section with a sentence that has troubled readers for two thousand years. "Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church" (Colossians 1:24). He is not saying Christ's atoning death was insufficient — the hymn he just sang made the cross the place where all things were reconciled. He is saying that the sufferings which carry that finished gospel out into the world are still being distributed, and he is glad to take his share. The affliction that delivers the message is ongoing; the atonement that is the message is complete. Paul gladly bears the cost of carrying a gospel whose payment is already made.

His whole commission, he says, is "to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints" (Colossians 1:26). He said it to the Ephesians in the same breath: he was sent "to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God" (Ephesians 3:9), and to the Romans he called it the mystery "kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed" (Romans 16:25-26). The pattern of Scripture is not a God who hoards and hides. It is a God who guarded a treasure for the right hour and then flung the doors open.

And the treasure is scandalously ordinary in its reach. "To them God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:27). Not Christ over you as a distant Lord. Not Christ before you as a moral example. Christ in you. The presence of the risen Son taking up residence in a Gentile believer no rabbi would have seated at his table. The hope of glory is not a reward you earn toward; it is a Person already dwelling within.

And hold the scandal of the word Gentiles a moment longer, because we read it flatly and Paul did not write it flatly. For a Jewish mind formed on centuries of separation, the riches of God's glory belonged inside the covenant, behind the temple veil, in the people set apart. That the indwelling Christ would take up residence in a Gentile — the outsider, the one on the wrong side of every wall — was the very thing hidden for ages that now stood revealed. The mystery is not only that Christ dwells in a person. It is that He dwells in the person no one expected Him to want. Paul is telling a church of nobodies in a backwater town that the treasure the initiated could not buy has been given to them, precisely to them, without qualification.

- **A. The mystery is a Person, not a secret technique.** The mystery religions sold knowledge. Paul preaches indwelling. You do not learn your way in; Christ moves in.
- **B. Paul's suffering is the delivery cost of a free gift.** "For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me" (Colossians 1:29). He spends himself so the gift arrives, and calls the spending joy.

### II. His Struggle Is for a Church Knit Together (Colossians 2:1-5)

Then Paul lets us see what he is actually praying for behind the labor. "For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face" (Colossians 2:1). The word is agōna — agony, the struggle of a contest. He agonizes for people he has never met. And what does he agonize toward? Not their comfort. Not even their doctrine in the abstract. "That their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God's mystery, which is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:2-3).

Knit together — sumbibasthentes, woven, bound into one fabric. Paul's ambition for the church is not that individuals privately thrive but that they be sewn to one another in love and, so bound, arrive at assurance. This is Paul the pastor, laboring like a mother, the way he told the Galatians: "my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you" (Galatians 4:19). The formation of Christ in a people is worth the anguish of childbirth to him.

And the reason he fights so hard against the false teachers is right here. "I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments" (Colossians 2:4). Plausible. The threat is never the obviously false. It is the persuasive, the reasonable-sounding, the argument that offers a treasure of wisdom somewhere other than in Christ — and Paul has just said that in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. There is no locked room of higher wisdom past Him. To go looking beyond Christ for the deeper thing is to walk away from the vault while standing inside it.

And Paul's phrase for the danger is worth weighing — "plausible arguments" (Colossians 2:4), pithanologia, persuasive speech, the reasoning that sounds right. He does not warn them against arguments that are obviously absurd. No one is deluded by the absurd. The threat to a church is always the teaching that keeps Christ and adds one reasonable-sounding thing, the supplement that seems only to enrich what they already have. That is why Paul writes from a distance to a church he has never met and agonizes as if the fire were in his own house. He knows how the counterfeit works. It never announces itself as a rival to Christ. It presents itself as the next step past Him — and the next step past the one in whom all the treasures are hidden is a step out of the treasury. Paul preached "Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), and he will pour out his life like a drink offering (Philippians 2:17) to keep a church from trading that wisdom for a plausible counterfeit.

- **A. Assurance comes through being knit together, not through solitary striving.** Paul ties full assurance to a church bound in love. The isolated Christian is the unassured Christian.
- **B. All the treasures are hidden in Christ, so every search for wisdom past Him is a search in the wrong room.** The false teacher does not deny Christ; he offers a supplement. The supplement is the lie.

### III. The Mystery With a Name in an Age of Endless Searching

We are a searching people who have forgotten what we are searching for. The spiritual marketplace has never been busier — the retreats, the practices, the imported wisdoms, the algorithm feeding us a fresh technique for meaning every morning. And the church has too often answered by baptizing the search rather than ending it, offering our own version of the deeper secret, the next level, the wisdom for the initiated. I have done it myself. I have stood in front of people hungry for a Person and handed them a program, a method, a plausible argument, because a technique is easier to deliver than a Christ who must be received. Paul's word for this is delusion, and the delusion is always plausible.

In the second century, a movement rose that named our hunger exactly. The Gnostics — the very word means the knowers — taught that salvation came through secret knowledge, gnōsis, available to the enlightened few who ascended past the material world through hidden wisdom. Around 180, a pastor in Lyon named Irenaeus wrote five books against them, and his answer was not a better secret. It was the scandal of the incarnation. The Word became flesh. God did not hide the treasure at the top of a ladder for the elite to climb; He came down and dwelt among us and now dwells in us. The Gnostic promised Christ plus the secret. Irenaeus, like Paul, insisted there is no plus. Christ in you is the treasure and the whole of it.

So the good news for a culture exhausted by its own seeking is that the seeking is over. Not because you found the answer, but because the answer found you and moved in. "Christ in you, the hope of glory." You do not have to ascend. You do not have to qualify for the inner circle. There is no inner circle — the doors are open, the mystery is preached in the street, and the risen Christ takes up residence in ordinary people who never saw Paul's face. The hope of glory is not a distant achievement you are climbing toward. It is a Person already present, and the anguished labor of every faithful pastor is simply to knit you to the others who carry Him, so that together you stop searching and start resting in the treasure you already hold.

- **A. A searching culture does not need a better search; it needs to be told the search is over.** We keep selling the next level to people standing inside the vault.
- **B. The hope of glory is Christ present, not glory pending.** He is not the reward at the end of the ladder. He is the one who came down it to live in you.

The mystery has a name.

## Rooted, Built Up, and Complete: The Fullness of Christ in Colossians 2:6-23
*Why the religion that looks the wisest can free no one*

**Text:** Colossians 2:6-23 · **Supporting:** Colossians 1:19; Galatians 3:3; Romans 6:4; Ephesians 2:8-9; 1 Timothy 4:8

There is a particular sadness in watching people work very hard at something that cannot save them. The strict diet of the soul. The calendar of observances. The rules layered on rules until the rules become the religion. It looks like seriousness. It looks like devotion. Paul looks at it and calls it captivity. The Colossians were being offered an upgrade — Christ, plus philosophy; Christ, plus the festivals; Christ, plus a punishing severity toward the body — and every version added something to Christ. Paul's whole answer is a subtraction. "In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him" (Colossians 2:9-10). You cannot add to fullness. Anything offered as a supplement to Christ is, by definition, a claim that Christ was not enough — and that claim is the oldest lie wearing its most religious face.

### I. Received Christ, So Walk in Him (Colossians 2:6-15)

Paul builds the whole section on the way they began. "As you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving" (Colossians 2:6-7). The images collide on purpose. Rooted is agricultural, a plant sunk deep; built up is architectural, a structure rising on a foundation. You continue the Christian life the way you started it — by receiving, not by achieving. He told the Galatians the same when they tried to finish in the flesh what they began in the Spirit: "Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?" (Galatians 3:3).

Notice that Paul gives them a verb of the whole self — "you received Christ Jesus the Lord." Not you received a set of teachings about Christ. Not you received an experience Christ made available. You received Him, the person, as Lord. And a person received is a person you go on relating to, not a transaction you completed and moved past. The rooting and the building-up are simply what receiving looks like over time. The plant does not root once and stop; it drives deeper every season. The building does not lay its foundation and quit; it rises. Continuance is not a second thing added to conversion. It is the same thing, still happening.

Then the warning, sharp and specific. "See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ. For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority" (Colossians 2:8-10). This is the hymn of chapter one cashed out into daily life. Because all the fullness of God dwells in Christ (Colossians 1:19), and because you are filled in Him, there is no deficiency for the supplement to fill. The head over every power cannot be improved by appeasing the powers.

And Paul grounds it in what happened at the cross with an image that should undo us. God "having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross" (Colossians 2:13-14). The record of debt — the cheirographon, the handwritten certificate of what we owed — was not renegotiated. It was nailed up and cancelled. "He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him" (Colossians 2:15). The very powers you were told to fear were led in a defeated procession behind the crucified Christ. We were buried with Him in baptism and raised with Him (Romans 6:4). The debt is paid, the powers are disarmed, and a paid debt cannot be paid again by our striving.

- **A. You continue as you began — by receiving fullness, not manufacturing it.** The Christian life is not Christ as the entrance and effort as the road.
- **B. The cross cancelled the debt and disarmed the powers, so both guilt and fear lose their grip.** Nothing remains to be added to a finished triumph.

### II. Do Not Submit to Shadows (Colossians 2:16-23)

So Paul draws the practical line. "Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ" (Colossians 2:16-17). A shadow is not nothing — it is cast by something real — but only a fool grasps at the shadow when the body has arrived. The dietary law and the festival calendar pointed forward to Christ; now that He has come, to be judged by the shadow is to face backward toward the very thing He fulfilled.

Paul names two more counterfeits, and both are worth watching, because they still wear their disguises well. The first is a mystical elitism — someone "insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind, and not holding fast to the Head" (Colossians 2:18-19). The tell is in the diagnosis: not holding fast to the Head. Every counterfeit spirituality, however elevated it sounds, has let go of Christ to grasp something adjacent to Him. The second is severity, and this is the one that fools the most sincere people. "If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations — 'Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch'?" (Colossians 2:20-21).

Then Paul delivers the verdict that ought to hang over every rigorous religion of self-improvement. "These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh" (Colossians 2:23). Read that last clause and let it land. The harsh regime looks wise. It looks like the serious option. And it accomplishes nothing against the actual disease. Paul told Timothy that "bodily training is of some value, but godliness is of value in every way" (1 Timothy 4:8) — and the self-made religion here is not even that. It is severity that flatters the ego while leaving the flesh untouched. Grace, not gritted teeth, is what saves: "by grace you have been saved through faith... not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9).

- **A. Shadows point to Christ; grasping the shadow means turning your back on the substance.** The old calendar was a signpost, not a destination.
- **B. Self-made severity has the appearance of wisdom and no power against the flesh.** It changes the diet and never the heart.

And sit with the strangeness of that final verdict, because it is one of the most counterintuitive sentences Paul ever wrote. We assume the danger runs the other direction — that the loose and the permissive endanger a soul, and the strict and the disciplined protect it. Paul says the severe religion is the one with no power against the flesh. Why? Because rules aimed at the body leave the heart's desires exactly where they were, and often feed the deepest desire of all, which is the desire to be the author of one's own righteousness. The ascetic starving his body may be gorging his pride. Severity can be the flesh's most convincing disguise — the sin of self-salvation wearing a hair shirt. That is why Paul says it has an appearance of wisdom. It looks like the opposite of self-indulgence, and it is self-indulgence at the deepest level, the indulgence of a self that will not be saved by grace because it insists on saving itself.

### III. The Wisest-Looking Religion in a Post-Christian Age Frees No One

We are told we have left religion behind, and we have not. We have only relocated it. The regimens of the age are not called religion, but watch how they function: the disciplines of the body pursued with monastic devotion, the purity codes of diet and consumption, the elaborate observances by which we prove ourselves clean and worthy and disciplined. Do not handle. Do not taste. Do not touch. The vocabulary is wellness now, but the structure is ancient — the belief that if I am severe enough with myself, I can master myself. And I have preached this too. I have stood in a pulpit and handed people a heavier yoke of religious effort and called it discipleship, dressing up self-made religion in the language of grace, because a rule is easier to give than a Savior is to trust.

Martin Luther knew this captivity from the inside. Before 1517, as an Augustinian monk, he punished his body with fasting and cold and endless confession, once confessing for six hours until his confessor grew weary of him, trying by severity to quiet a conscience that would not be quiet. It never worked. The appearance of wisdom, and no power against the flesh — Paul had diagnosed Luther's monastery a millennium and a half early. What finally freed him was not a stricter rule but a single line from Romans and the discovery Paul makes here: that the record of debt was already nailed to the cross, that he was already filled in Christ, that there was nothing left to add. The severity had been a way of paying a debt already paid.

This is why the gospel is harder to believe than any religion of effort. Effort lets us keep the ledger and keep our pride; grace takes both away. The self-made religion of our age will always look wiser than trust, because trust looks like doing nothing while Christ does everything. But you were buried with Him and raised with Him. The debt is cancelled. The powers are disarmed. And every regimen you have taken up to make yourself acceptable is a shadow you are grasping at while the substance stands in the room, saying you were complete before you started. You cannot add to fullness. Stop trying to earn what He already gave.

- **A. We renamed religion as wellness and self-mastery, but the structure of works never changed.** The ledger is the same; only the vocabulary updated.
- **B. Christ cancelled the debt, so the striving is not devotion — it is unbelief in disguise.** Fullness cannot be supplemented, only received.

You are complete in Him.

## Seek the Things Above: The Risen Life in Colossians 3:1-17
*What changes when your real life is hidden where no one can reach it*

**Text:** Colossians 3:1-17 · **Supporting:** Romans 6:11; Galatians 3:27-28; Ephesians 4:22-24; Matthew 6:21; 2 Corinthians 5:17

Paul has spent two chapters dismantling every counterfeit — the philosophy, the calendar, the severity to the body — and a reader might expect him to land on a new set of rules to replace the old ones. He does the opposite. Before he says do anything, he tells you what is already true. "If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God" (Colossians 3:1). The command rests on an accomplished fact. You have been raised. The Christian life is not a project of climbing toward a resurrection you hope to earn; it is the working-out of a resurrection that already happened to you, joined to Christ. And the strangest, most freeing thing Paul says is where your real life now is: not in your grip, not in your performance, not even in your feelings. "Your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3).

### I. Set Your Mind Above, Because You Have Died and Been Raised (Colossians 3:1-4)

"For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory" (Colossians 3:3-4). Two verbs govern everything after: you died, you were raised. This is the pattern Paul gave the Romans — "consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" (Romans 6:11). Not aspire to be dead to sin. Consider yourselves already dead to it, because in Christ's death you died and in His resurrection you were raised.

And because that is true, Paul commands the mind before the hands. "Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth" (Colossians 3:2). The word is phroneite — the settled orientation of the mind, what you reckon with, what you organize your attention around. This is not escapism, a spiritual daydreaming that ignores the earth. It is the discovery that the center of gravity of your life has moved. Your treasure has relocated, and the Lord said it plainly: "where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21). If your true life is now seated with Christ at God's right hand, then that is where your mind belongs, because that is where you actually are.

And notice the mercy in the word hidden. Your life is not on display, subject to the verdict of the crowd or the market or your own worst day. It is hidden with Christ in God — the safest possible place, sealed away from every power that could reach it. The performance of the self that exhausts us all is beside the point, because the self that matters is not up for review. It is hidden. It will appear only when Christ appears, and then it will appear in glory.

And Paul says something even more startling than that your life is hidden. He says Christ is your life — "when Christ who is your life appears" (Colossians 3:4). Not Christ who improves your life. Not Christ who gives your life meaning, as if you had a life running independently that He came to enrich. Christ is the life. Take Him away and there is no residual self left standing that merely lost its purpose. The self that will last is the self joined to Him and hidden in Him, and there is no other. This is why the command to seek the things above is not a demand to leave your life behind for something loftier. It is a command to look toward where your life actually is now. You are not being asked to abandon yourself. You are being told where your true self went.

- **A. The command to seek above rests on the fact that you were raised, not the hope that you might be.** Effort follows identity; it never creates it.
- **B. A hidden life is a secure life.** What is hidden with Christ in God cannot be lost, exposed, or condemned by anyone below.

### II. Put to Death the Old, Put On the New (Colossians 3:5-17)

Only now, on the ground of that accomplished resurrection, does Paul turn to conduct — and even here the imperative flows from the indicative. "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry" (Colossians 3:5). Put to death — because you already died. He is telling you to make real in your body what is already true in Christ. "Put away" anger, wrath, malice, slander, obscene talk; "do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self" (Colossians 3:8-10). The clothing image is deliberate. Paul told the Ephesians to "put off your old self... and put on the new self, created after the likeness of God" (Ephesians 4:22-24). You take off the old life like a garment you have outgrown and put on the new like a robe already hanging ready for you.

Then Paul says something that would have detonated a first-century room. In the new self, "there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all" (Colossians 3:11). Echoing Galatians — "you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28) — he tears down the deepest social walls of the ancient world in a single line. The new humanity does not run on the old sortings. Christ is all, and in all.

The pairing of Scythian and barbarian is the sharpest of them. To a cultured Greek, barbarian named anyone outside Greek civilization, and Scythian named the barbarian's barbarian — the byword for the savage and the untouchable, the person at the very bottom of the ancient world's contempt. Paul reaches for exactly that name and says it too has been erased in the new self. The categories we use to rank one another — refined and crude, insider and outsider, our kind and the kind we would never — do not survive the resurrection. Christ did not merely add a new group to the top of the list. He took away the list. When Paul says Christ is all and in all, he means there is no longer a scale on which one Christian stands above another, because the only measure left is a Christ who is equally the life of every one of them.

And the new garment has a specific cut. "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony" (Colossians 3:12-14). The measure of our forgiving is His forgiving of us — never our sense of what the offender deserves. And over all of it, love, the binding fabric. "Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts... Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly" (Colossians 3:15-16). Rule — brabeuetō, the word for an umpire's decisive call. Dwell richly — take up abundant residence. The new self is not white-knuckled behavior. It is Christ's peace umpiring the heart and Christ's word living inside it, so that "whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus" (Colossians 3:17).

- **A. Every command to change is grounded in a change already made.** "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation" (2 Corinthians 5:17) — you put to death the old because you are, in fact, new.
- **B. Forgiveness is measured by the cross, not by the offense.** "As the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive" removes the ledger from our hands.

### III. Where the Mind Rests in a Culture of the Curated Self

We live in the most self-conscious age in human history. The self is the great project — assembled, displayed, defended, revised in real time before an audience we cannot see and cannot satisfy. We are told to look within to find who we are, and then to broadcast it, and then to guard it against every threat. And the exhaustion is total, because a self that lives on display can never rest. It is always up for review. I know this from inside a pulpit, where the temptation to curate a self for a congregation is constant, where I have set my mind on how I am being received rather than on Christ seated above, tending the image instead of resting in the one that is hidden. Paul cuts the whole thing off at the root. Your real life is not on the screen. It is hidden with Christ in God.

The ancient church knew a discipline we have lost. When the desert fathers withdrew to the Egyptian wilderness in the fourth century — Antony going out around 270, and the movement swelling after him — they were not running from the world so much as refusing the frantic performance of the self that the late Roman city demanded. Their word was not escape; it was watchfulness. They set the mind above by starving it of the endless input below, and out of that stillness came a depth the noisy could not reach. Whatever we make of the extremes of the desert, they understood Paul's command that the noise-drunk self cannot: you cannot set your mind on things above while it is chained to the ceaseless scroll of things below.

The gospel's answer to the exhausting project of the self is not a better self-image. It is a hidden one. You do not have to construct an identity and defend it to the death, because Christ is your life, and that life is sealed in God where no critic and no failure and no algorithm can touch it. "When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory." The verdict is already in, hidden, waiting. So you are free to put to death the covetousness and the slander and the performance — not to earn a self, but because the self that matters is already secure, already loved, already raised. Stop building what Christ has already hidden. Set your mind where you actually are.

- **A. A curated self is a self that can never rest, because it lives before a crowd that never renders a final verdict.** Christ has already rendered it, and hidden the result in God.
- **B. Watchfulness above frees us from the frantic performance below.** The mind set above is not less present on earth; it is finally free to be.

Set your mind above.

## The Lordship of Christ in House and Prayer: The Ordinary Made Holy in Colossians 3:18-4:18
*How the supremacy of Christ reaches the kitchen, the workplace, and the names in the margin*

**Text:** Colossians 3:18-4:18 · **Supporting:** Ephesians 6:5-9; Philemon 1:16; 1 Corinthians 10:31; Colossians 1:17; Matthew 5:16

Paul has taken us to the summit — the image of the invisible God, the fullness of deity dwelling bodily, all things holding together in Christ, the risen life hidden in God. And now, having climbed to the highest doctrine in the New Testament, he brings it down the stairs and sets it in the kitchen. Wives and husbands. Children and parents. Slaves and masters. The way you work when no one is watching. The letter that began with the cosmos ends with a shopping list of names — real coworkers, greeting real people, in a real town. This is not Paul running out of grand things to say. This is the whole point. A Christ who holds together all things but not your Tuesday is not the Christ of this letter. The supremacy of the Son reaches into the ordinary or it does not reach at all.

### I. Every Relationship Rendered to the Lord (Colossians 3:18-4:1)

Paul addresses the household in pairs, and a modern reader tenses at the first word — "Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord" (Colossians 3:18). But watch what he does that no ancient household code did: he addresses the ones without power, treats them as moral agents responsible to God, and then binds the powerful with equal weight. "Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them" (Colossians 3:19). "Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). In a world where the paterfamilias held absolute authority, Paul turns to the man and limits him — do not be harsh, do not provoke. The one with the power is put under the Lord first.

Then he spends the most words on the ones with the least power at all. "Slaves, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters... fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men" (Colossians 3:22-23). Paul is not blessing the institution of slavery — in the very letter he carries alongside this one, to Philemon, he tells a master to receive his returning slave Onesimus "no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother" (Philemon 1:16), a sentence that plants the charge that would one day blow the institution apart. What Paul is doing here is relocating the audience of every act. The slave with no earthly dignity is told he serves the Lord Christ and will receive the inheritance — and then the master is warned, "you also have a Master in heaven" (Colossians 4:1). The word for it is in Ephesians too: masters, do the same to them, "knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him" (Ephesians 6:9).

There is a phrase in the middle of the slave's instruction that quietly overturns everything around it — "knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance" (Colossians 3:24). Under Roman law, a slave could inherit nothing; the slave was property, not heir. And Paul tells the person the law calls property that the Lord will give him the inheritance. He hands the legal nonentity the one thing his world said he could never hold. This is not Paul making peace with the system. This is Paul reaching under the system and cutting the cord that held it to the conscience, telling the slave that his true status is fixed in heaven by a Master with no partiality, and telling the master that his authority is on loan and audited. A doctrine like that cannot coexist forever with the institution it addresses. It is a seed planted under a wall.

This is the doctrine of Christ's supremacy landing where it costs. "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ" (Colossians 3:23-24). Every duty, however invisible, is rendered to a Lord who sees it. "Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31).

- **A. Paul dignifies the powerless as moral agents and puts the powerful under the Lord first.** The household code does not sanctify hierarchy; it subjects everyone in it to Christ.
- **B. The audience of every act is relocated from people to the Lord.** Work done for the Lord cannot be demeaning, because the one it is rendered to is not demeaned.

### II. A Life of Watchful Prayer and Clear Witness (Colossians 4:2-18)

Having grounded conduct, Paul turns the whole church outward, and he starts with prayer. "Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving" (Colossians 4:2). Watchful — grēgorountes, alert, awake, the posture of a sentry. Prayer is not a mood; it is a vigilance. And even from prison, what Paul asks for himself is not release but opportunity: "that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison" (Colossians 4:3). The man in chains prays for an open door, not an open cell.

And he asks the church to pray the same for him — "pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word... that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak" (Colossians 4:3-4). Consider what he does not request. Not comfort. Not vindication. Not that the people who imprisoned an innocent man be dealt with. He asks for clarity, that when the door opens he will not fumble the one thing he was put on earth to say. A man whose treasure has been relocated above prays differently than a man whose treasure is here, because he is no longer asking heaven to rearrange his circumstances. He is asking heaven to use them. The prison is not an interruption of Paul's ministry; Paul has decided it is a pulpit with a lock on it, and he wants only that the door open long enough to preach.

Then the witness. "Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person" (Colossians 4:5-6). Notice the balance — gracious and salted, warm and with an edge, wise toward the outsider without being ashamed before him. This is the Lord's own charge that our light "shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 5:16), scaled to the reality of a small church surrounded by a watching, unpersuaded city.

And then Paul does the thing that ought to stop us. He lists the names. Tychicus, the beloved brother. Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother — the runaway slave, named as a brother in the same breath as an apostle's envoy. Aristarchus, his fellow prisoner. Mark. Justus. Epaphras, always struggling in prayer for them. Luke, the beloved physician. Nympha and the church in her house. Archippus, given a personal charge to fulfill his ministry. "I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains" (Colossians 4:18). The cosmic hymn ends in a roll call of ordinary saints who carried the gospel together, and that is not an afterthought. It is the proof. In Christ all things hold together (Colossians 1:17) — including this small, named, unglamorous fellowship of people who worked and prayed and suffered side by side.

- **A. Even in chains, Paul prays for an open door, not an open cell.** The supremacy of Christ reorders what we ask for.
- **B. The letter of the cosmos ends in a list of names, because the body is where the doctrine becomes flesh.** Real coworkers, remembered by name, are the gospel bearing fruit.

### III. The Sacredness of the Ordinary in a Culture That Worships the Platform

We have built a culture that reserves meaning for the visible. The platform. The audience. The brand. The measurable impact that can be counted and displayed. And the church breathed it in without noticing, until we too began to believe that the significant work of God happens on a stage and the ordinary Christian in the ordinary week is, at best, support staff for the people with microphones. I have preached this without meaning to. I have honored the visible ministry from a pulpit and quietly implied that the mother in the kitchen and the man at the loading dock were the audience for the real thing, rather than the place where the real thing happens. Paul's list of names is a rebuke to every one of us who measures the kingdom by its platforms.

The monastic movement recovered this when the church had nearly lost it. When Benedict of Nursia wrote his Rule around 530, in the wreckage of a collapsing Roman order, he gave his monks a phrase that has outlived every empire since: ora et labora, pray and work. And he insisted — against the assumption that the sacred lived only in the chapel — that the tools of the monastery were to be treated "as if they were the sacred vessels of the altar." The kitchen knife was holy. The garden hoe was holy. The labor of the ordinary hour was rendered to the Lord and therefore no less sacred than the liturgy. Benedict had simply believed what Paul wrote to Colossae: whatever you do, do it heartily, as for the Lord.

This is where the supremacy of Christ finally lands, and it lands on you. Not on the platform you do not have, but on the work you do have — the diaper changed at three in the morning, the shift worked with integrity when the manager is gone, the marriage tended when no one applauds, the prayer prayed by a name no one will remember. Christ is Lord of all of it or He is Lord of none of it, and the whole letter has been driving to this: the one in whom the fullness of deity dwells bodily is the Lord of your kitchen. He receives the invisible act. He records the unphotographed faithfulness. And He is knitting a body together out of ordinary, named people who serve Him where no one is watching, which is exactly where He has always done His deepest work. The platform will not save you and it cannot sanctify you. Your Master is in heaven, and He is watching the ordinary.

- **A. We reserved meaning for the visible, and the kingdom runs on the invisible.** The named saints of Colossians 4 had no platform and carried the gospel anyway.
- **B. Christ's lordship makes the ordinary sacred, because the ordinary is rendered to Him.** The kitchen and the loading dock are altars when the work is done for the Lord.

Whatever you do, do it for Him.
